author: Kapil Kajal
title: Pearl Harbor to become first US Navy base armed with hypersonic destroyers, submarines - NewsBreak
text:
By Kapil Kajal ,
2 days ago
The U.S. Navy is repositioning some of its most advanced warships and submarines to Hawaii as part of a major modernization effort aimed at countering China’s growing military presence in the Pacific.
The move will make Pearl Harbor the home of the Navy’s first hypersonic-armed surface and undersea fleet by 2030, officials said.
The initiative centers on deploying ships and submarines equipped with the Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) weapon, the Navy’s first sea-launched hypersonic missile.
By placing these high-speed strike assets closer to contested waters near Taiwan and the South China Sea, the service aims to cut response times by days and bolster deterrence in one of the world’s most volatile regions.
By homeporting these vessels in Hawaii, the Navy is significantly improving its ability to project power and respond quickly to emerging threats in the Indo-Pacific.
A hypersonic hub in the Pacific According to service planning documents and reports from Naval News , the Navy intends to base all three Zumwalt-class destroyers and several Virginia-class submarines armed with CPS weapons at Joint Base Pearl Harbor–Hickam.
Infrastructure upgrades, including new electrical systems and wharf improvements, are already underway to accommodate the advanced platforms.
The shift represents a fundamental reorientation of the Navy’s strike doctrine, concentrating its most time-sensitive capabilities closer to potential flashpoints.
Each Zumwalt destroyer will eventually carry 12 hypersonic missiles. In contrast, new Virginia-class submarines with the Virginia Payload Module (VPM) will carry the same number, providing long-range strike options across air, land, and maritime domains.
Much of the modernization work at Pearl Harbor is scheduled for completion by mid-2028, with the full complement of CPS-capable ships and submarines in place by the end of the decade.
The Navy’s futuristic Zumwalt-class destroyers, originally built for shore bombardment and stealth operations, have been reimagined as hypersonic strike platforms.
Each features an advanced “tumblehome” hull design, composite structures, and massive electrical generation capacity intended for future directed-energy weapons such as lasers or railguns.
“The Zumwalts have the power, the stealth, and the internal space to integrate the weapons of tomorrow,” a senior Navy engineer said. “They’re the right hull for this mission.”
The program’s initial gun systems proved too costly to sustain, but the ships’ large launch cells and modular design make them well-suited for CPS integration.
Numbers and limits Retired Rear Adm. Joe Sestak, a former carrier strike group commander, reportedly called the move “a smart step” but warned about the limited number of missiles available.
“These hypersonic missiles, nobody has a defense against them,” Sestak said. “But with just 12 per ship, you’re not going to stop an invasion with that. Redundancy and volume matter in a real war.”
With three Zumwalts and several Virginia-class submarines, the Navy will likely field fewer than 60 hypersonic missiles from Hawaii by 2030, a fraction of what might be required in a large-scale conflict.
Sestak said CPS could play a decisive role in two scenarios: a Chinese blockade of Taiwan or a full-scale amphibious invasion. In either case, commanders will face hard choices about targeting.
“Do you strike the invasion ports or the surface combatants? You can’t hit everything,” he said. “But whatever you hit, they can’t defend against it.”
While hypersonic weapons promise near-uninterceptable speed and range, defenses remain limited. Japan is advancing a ship-mounted railgun, while Israel’s Rafael and Lockheed Martin are developing a maritime variant of the Iron Beam laser system.
The Zumwalt’s enormous power reserves make it a potential host for these directed-energy defenses, which could eventually counter hypersonic threats as effectively as they launch them.
“To have missile defense that can handle both ballistic and hypersonic threats, that would be an awesome capability,” Sestak said.
The Hawaii realignment reflects a broader U.S. effort to harden its Pacific posture, reduce response times, and integrate advanced systems under the Navy’s distributed operations doctrine.
Pearl Harbor’s transformation into a forward strike hub is both a technological and strategic gamble, one that hinges on limited munitions, reliable networks, and emerging defenses.
Whether it’s enough to deter China will depend less on how fast the missiles fly than on how effectively commanders use them when the time comes.
